The glassback has six limbs. Four stout legs carry its weight; two smaller front limbs end in flexible, three-pronged “hands.” It uses these to pull up tough marsh plants, scrape bacterial mats from rocks, and pry shell-like creatures out of the mud. Its mouth is a blunt, muscular beak lined with ridged plates rather than teeth. These grind food into a paste, which is further broken down by bacteria living in the animal’s long gut. The microbes help it digest fibrous plants and neutralize some of the marsh’s high salt content.

Its most striking feature is a pair of tall, translucent sails rising from its shoulders. Veins fan through each sail, carrying blood close to the surface. When the animal is overheated, it spreads them to lose heat in the coastal wind. At dawn and dusk, the sails also display shifting bands of color. The patterns are produced by layers of pigment cells that expand and contract, so a glassback can signal its mood without making a sound. A broad, calm ripple means “I am feeding here.” A sharp, flashing zigzag is a warning.

Glassbacks perceive the world in ways that are unfamiliar to us. Their eyes are small and dark, but sensitive to polarized light; they can pick out the glimmer of a predator’s scales against the glare of a tidal pool. Fine hairs around the mouth and forelimbs detect tiny movements in water and mud. They also feel vibrations through their feet. A glassback may stop feeding, all six limbs rigid, because it has sensed the distant footfalls of another animal through the flats.

At high tide, it wades into the shallows to feed, closing valves over its breathing slits and drawing air into a pair of internal lungs. It can remain underwater for nearly an hour, moving slowly among the reeds. When the tide retreats, it follows the waterline, leaving broad, six-toed tracks in the wet sand. If startled, it folds its sails flat, tucks its head beneath its armored shoulders, and braces itself in the mud. Most small predators cannot shift it. Larger ones must overturn it, a difficult task in the sucking ground of the flats.

Glassbacks gather to breed during Veyra’s longest low-tide season. Males and females circle one another, tapping their front limbs against the ground in a slow rhythm that carries through the mud. After mating, the female digs a warm nest above the usual high-water mark and lays a dozen leathery eggs. She guards them until they hatch, then leads the young toward shallow pools.

Newly hatched glassbacks are only hand-sized. They have feathery gills along their necks and soft, nearly transparent plates. For their first months they live in water, feeding on microscopic life. As they grow, the gills shrink and the lungs strengthen; their armor darkens and hardens, and their sails unfold. A young glassback stays near its mother for almost a year, learning which pools are safe and how to read the tide.

Seen from a distance, a herd crossing the flats looks like a procession of small, shifting sails. Up close, each animal moves with patient deliberation, testing the mud before placing a foot. They are not fast, but they are difficult to surprise—and on a world where the shore is never in the same place for long, patience is a powerful adaptation.
